title: Vou a Sintra — ir, vir, sair, and how to get there
goal: Master the three most common verbs of movement, choose between *ir a* and *ir para*, and invite people along with *vamos*.
bekal: say the forms of *ir*, *vir* and *sair* without hesitating
name means of transport with the right preposition

dialogs.title: Diálogo — Um passeio a Sintra
dialogs.intro: The night before, Ana calls Budi to invite him on a day trip to Sintra.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Amanhã vou a Sintra. Vens comigo?
lines.id: Tomorrow I'm going to Sintra. Want to come with me?
lines.literal: tomorrow I-go to Sintra. you-come with-me?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vou, claro! Como é que vamos? De comboio?
lines.id: Sure I'm coming! How are we getting there? By train?
lines.literal: I-go, clear! how is it that we-go? by train?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Vamos de comboio até Sintra e depois de autocarro até ao palácio.
lines.id: We'll take the train to Sintra and then the bus up to the palace.
lines.literal: we-go by train until Sintra and after by bus until to-the palace.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: A que horas sais de casa?
lines.id: What time are you leaving home?
lines.literal: at what hours you-leave from home?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Saio às oito. O comboio parte do Rossio às oito e meia.
lines.id: I'm leaving at 8:00. The train leaves Rossio at 8:30.
lines.literal: I-leave at-the(pl) eight. the train departs from-the Rossio at-the(pl) eight and half.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Vou, sim. Passo por tua casa às oito menos um quarto.
lines.id: Yes. I'll come by your place at a quarter to eight.
lines.literal: I-go, yes. I-pass by your house at-the(pl) eight minus a quarter.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Great. And when do we come back?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Voltamos ao fim da tarde. Vamos almoçar lá.
lines.id: We'll come back late in the afternoon. We'll have lunch there.
lines.literal: we-return at-the end of-the afternoon. we-go to-lunch there.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Então vou levar a máquina fotográfica.
lines.literal: then I-go to-take the machine photographic.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Leva! Sintra é linda. Vais gostar muito.
lines.id: Bring it! Sintra is beautiful. You're going to love it.
lines.literal: take! Sintra is beautiful. you-go to-like much.

notes: **Vou a Sintra, with a.** The preposition *a* is used for trips **with a return**: visits, outings, going to the office or to school. *Para* is used for going somewhere **to stay**, or at least for a long time: *vou para o Brasil* (I'm moving to Brazil). The difference matters: *vou a Portugal* means a vacation, *vou para Portugal* means moving there.

**Vamos has two meanings at once:** "we go" and "let's". *Vamos!* on its own means "let's go!", and *Vamos almoçar* means "let's have lunch" — not just "we're going to have lunch". Context tells them apart, and the Portuguese are never confused.

**Vens buscar-me?** — *ir/vir buscar* means to pick someone up or fetch something. It's a typically Portuguese construction that can't be translated word for word: literally "come to-look-for me". *Vou buscar o pão* = I'll go get the bread.

**Vais gostar** — *ir* + infinitive is the most common way to talk about the future in conversation, just like English "going to". It's covered in full in Unit 19; for now, recognize that *vou comer* means "I'm going to eat", not "I'm going off to eat".
**Então** means "then" or "so", and it sits at the start or end of a sentence. The Portuguese also use it as a casual greeting among friends: *Então? Tudo bem?* — roughly "So? All good?"
**Leva!** is the command form of *levar*. Commands for *tu* with *-ar* verbs end in **-a**: *fala!*, *leva!*, *espera!*. For *-er* and *-ir* verbs they end in **-e**: *come!*, *abre!*.

grammars.title: Ir — to go, and "going to"
body: Irregular, and it looks nothing like its infinitive. Luckily it has only five forms, and they're all short.
after: **Ir a** = go and come back. **Ir para** = go to stay. **Ir de** = go by (transport). All three can appear in one sentence: *Vou a Sintra de comboio.*
Place names with an article fuse with it: *vou **ao** mercado*, *vou **à** escola*, *vou **ao** Porto*. But *vou a Lisboa*, *vou a Portugal* — no contraction, because those names take no article.

grammars.title: Vir and sair
body: *Vir* is the opposite of *ir*: to come toward the speaker. *Sair* means to go out or leave, and also "to go out" for fun.
after: **Vem and vêm** differ only by the ^ accent in writing — just like *tem* and *têm* in Unit 5. The pattern repeats, so learn it once: a ^ on short words like these marks the **plural**.
*Sair* also means going out at night: *Sais hoje à noite?* = "Are you going out tonight?" *Sair com alguém* means to date someone.
*Sair de* (to leave from) and *sair para* (to leave for): *saio de casa às oito*, *saio para o trabalho*.

grammars.title: Comigo, contigo — when com fuses
body: The preposition *com* fuses with personal pronouns, and the forms must be memorized because they can't be guessed.
after: Only three forms really fuse: *comigo*, *contigo*, *connosco*. The rest stay separate.
Note the spelling **connosco** with two n's — that's the Portuguese spelling. In Brazil it's written *conosco*.

blocks.title: Levar or trazer?
items: *Levar* means taking something **away** from where the speaker is — the same direction as *ir*. *Levo o guarda-chuva* = I'll take my umbrella (with me).
*Trazer* means bringing something **toward** where the speaker is — the same direction as *vir*. *Trazes o mapa?* = will you bring the map (here)?
English "take" and "bring" work the same way in principle, but English speakers often blur them. Quick check: if you could swap in *ir*, use *levar*; if *vir*, use *trazer*.
